desc:
In base b, a positive integer with k digits is narcissistic when the sum of its base-b digits, each raised to the power k, equals the integer itself. In base 10 this is the familiar Armstrong number: 153 = 13 + 53 + 33.

Given a base b and a limit n, return how many narcissistic integers from 1 to n there are. Every single digit is narcissistic, since a digit d equals d1.

b = 10, n = 400    -> 12   (1 to 9, plus 153, 370 and 371)
b = 2,  n = 1000   -> 1    (only the number 1)
hints: Scanning every number up to n and converting it to base b is slow for large n. Instead use the fact that a k-digit number is at least b<sup>k-1</sup> and at most k * (b-1)<sup>k</sup>.
A narcissistic number is determined by the multiset of its digits: its value is the sum of the k-th powers of those digits. So you can enumerate multisets of k digits instead of numbers.

For each length k with b<sup>k-1</sup> at most n, enumerate all multisets of k digits from 0 to b-1, compute s as the sum of d<sup>k</sup>, and count s when it is at most n and its base-b digits form the same multiset.
editorial: Let a k-digit narcissistic number be x. Its value is the sum of the k-th powers of its digits, so the multiset of its digits determines x. Conversely, every multiset M of k digits gives a candidate s, the sum of d<sup>k</sup> over M. The candidate is narcissistic exactly when s has k base-b digits that form M again. Each narcissistic number comes from exactly one multiset, so counting valid multisets counts numbers once.

The number of k-element multisets from b symbols is C(b + k - 1, k). For n up to 10,000,000 the largest length is k = 8, and in base 10 that is only C(17, 8) = 24,310 multisets. The check s ≤ n removes most of them before any digit work is done.
Single digits need care. For k = 1 the multiset {d} gives s = d, which is counted for every d from 1 to b-1. The value 0 is excluded because the numbers must be positive.
time: O(sum over k of C(b+k-1, k) * k)
